nature-eco-347.title: Ecological stoichiometry: the chemistry of eating
nature-eco-347.text: Termites have a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of about 5, yet they eat wood with a ratio of 300–1000. Ecological stoichiometry studies mismatches like this: how the balance of energy and chemical elements shapes living things and their interactions in ecosystems. Plants and algae vary widely in their elemental make-up. Animals keep a nearly fixed composition, a trait called stoichiometric homeostasis. In lakes, algae and {{ref:nature-eco-709}}, dead organic matter, range in carbon-to-phosphorus ratio from 100 to 1000. The zooplankton Daphnia stays near 80:1. Nitrogen and phosphorus pollution from farming can boost stream producers and ripple up the food web.

nature-eco-371.title: Host–parasite coevolution: an evolving relationship
nature-eco-371.text: A parasite that kills its only host too soon destroys its own future. A parasite with a single host is pushed toward being more benign, even mutualistic, because it can reproduce longer if its host lives longer. That is one force in the way hosts and parasites evolve together and change their relationship over time. Another force pushes the opposite way. Competition between parasites tends to favor faster-reproducing, more virulent strains, those that do more harm. Hosts fight back with skin barriers, immune systems, grooming and, in plants, chemical defenses.

nature-eco-375.title: Population ecology: births, deaths, arrivals and departures
nature-eco-375.text: A population changes in only four ways: individuals are born, die, arrive or leave. Population ecology studies those changes, through births, deaths, immigration and emigration, and how populations interact with their environment. Its bookkeeping fits on one line: N1 = N0 + B − D + I − E. The new number is the starting number, plus births, minus deaths, plus immigrants, minus emigrants. Population size is the number of individuals, and population density is how closely packed they are. The largest population an environment's resources can sustain is its {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. The field began with Malthus's model, in which a population in a constant environment grows or declines exponentially. Fisheries and wildlife managers track three rates: {{ref:nature-eco-590}}, growth and mortality, including deaths from harvesting. {{ref:nature-eco-760}} also grew from this field. It predicts a species' long-term chance of persisting in a patch of suitable land, and it matters for conservation.

nature-eco-380.title: Predation: the hunter and the hunted
nature-eco-380.text: Lynx and snowshoe hare numbers rise and fall in cycles, and the way predators and prey interact may explain why. Predation is an interaction in which one organism, the predator, kills and eats another, its prey. It belongs to a family of feeding behaviors along with parasitism and parasitoidism. It overlaps with plant eating when animals destroy seeds. To feed, a predator must search for, pursue and kill its prey, weighing costs and benefits at each step. Predators limit prey both by eating them and by changing how they behave. Without predators, a prey population can grow exponentially until it nears its {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. Predators also shape ecosystems indirectly by changing the behavior of plant-eating animals, as wolves do for riverside plants and sea otters for kelp. By stopping any one species from becoming dominant, some predators raise biodiversity. Such predators are called keystone species.

nature-eco-440.title: Green and blue infrastructure: building nature into cities
nature-eco-440.text: Buildings certified under LEED, a rating system for environmentally friendly buildings, report using 30% less energy and gaining economic and mental benefits from natural light. Infrastructure of this kind, described in {{ref:nature-nbs-161}} and {{ref:nature-nbs-162}}, means building in ways that weave natural systems such as vegetation and water into human-made structures. The green side includes nature preserves and added vegetation such as vertical gardens. The blue side includes ways of managing rainwater, such as planted channels that soak up runoff ({{ref:nature-nbs-174}}).

nature-eco-452.title: Agroecosystems: nature reshaped to grow food
nature-eco-452.text: Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest and most resilient agroecosystem. An agroecosystem is a natural ecosystem that people have modified and manage to produce crops or livestock. Like any ecosystem, it combines a physical environment, living things such as crops and wildlife, and the interactions linking them. It is the basic unit of study in {{ref:nature-nbs-246}} and {{ref:nature-nbs-258}}. Its reach goes beyond the farm gate, to the whole region its activity affects through changes to species, energy flows and nutrient balance. Intensively managed farms simplify those flows, and their excess nutrients cause eutrophication, an overgrowth of algae, downstream. More plant diversity brings both ecological and economic benefits. Some approaches try to blur the line with natural ecosystems, for example through growing several crops together, wildlife buffer strips and {{ref:nature-nbs-292}}. A report by the International Water Management Institute and UNEP suggested assigning value to ecosystems and recognizing trade-offs among their users.

nature-eco-520.title: Drylands: where water is the limit
nature-eco-520.text: Drylands cover 41.3% of Earth's land surface, including 66% of Africa, 40% of Asia, 24% of Europe and 15% of Latin America. They are lands defined by scarce water, where rainfall is balanced by evaporation and the water plants give off. The UN Environment Programme defines them as tropical and temperate areas where the {{ref:nature-eco-686}} is below 0.65. It compares rainfall with the water the air could draw off; the lower it is, the drier the land. More than 2 billion people live in drylands, and 72% of drylands lie in developing countries. They include 45% of the world's agricultural land. Their behaviour depends on many linked interactions among climate, soil and vegetation. Unlike humid biomes, drylands move water around mainly through surface runoff. They are highly vulnerable to climate change through shifting rainfall and land degradation.

nature-eco-572.title: Biological dispersal: leaving home to spread out
nature-eco-572.text: Leaving home is a gamble for any living thing. Biological dispersal is the movement of living things, or their seeds and spores, away from where they were born. They move to where they breed, or from one breeding site to another. Technically, it is any movement that could lead to the spread of genes between populations. It runs in three phases: departure, transfer and settlement. Organisms disperse when the benefits outweigh the costs. The benefits include new resources and escape from competition and inbreeding. The costs come in energy, risk, time and lost opportunity. The consequences are large. Dispersal shapes how populations grow and shrink, how their genes vary, and where species live. Ecosystems depend on individuals moving between patches of habitat, which makes dispersal critical to their stability. It even counts as a service. The carrying of seeds, and the ability to disperse at all, are treated as ecosystem services and as part of a species' capacity to adapt to {{ref:nature-hist-007}}.

nature-eco-588.title: R/K selection: many cheap offspring or a few costly ones
nature-eco-588.text: A dandelion and an elephant follow opposite strategies for passing on their genes. R/K selection theory is an evolutionary hypothesis that species are selected either to produce many cheap offspring or a few offspring with heavy parental investment. The letters come from the logistic model, where r is the maximum growth rate and K the {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. r-selection dominates in unstable environments. It favors many offspring, small size, early maturity and wide dispersal, as in dandelions. K-selection dominates in stable environments. It favors strong competitors with large bodies, long lives and few well-cared-for young, such as elephants and whales. Most organisms mix the traits. MacArthur and Wilson coined the terms in 1967. The theory was popular in the 1970s and 1980s, then lost ground after empirical studies contradicted its predictions. {{ref:nature-eco-754}}, based on how death rates vary with age, has replaced it, and some now speak of fast versus slow life histories. The stakes are practical. Slow-breeding, long-lived species such as orange roughy proved vulnerable to fishing models that assumed faster growth.

nature-eco-659.title: Algal blooms
nature-eco-659.text: An algal bloom is a rapid increase or accumulation in the population of algae in fresh or marine water. Blooms follow nutrients such as nitrogen or phosphorus, from fertilizer washed off farmland or other nutrient pollution, entering the water and causing excessive algal growth. There is no officially recognized threshold: definitions have used chlorophyll above 5-100 ug/L or more than 1000 cells/mL of the blooming species. Marine blooms rise each spring as storms add nutrients to sunlit water. Satellites track them via chlorophyll, and they end when nutrients decline and zooplankton graze. Bloom intensity and occurrence have increased in recent decades, mainly because warming water stimulates growth and lengthens the season. Heavy rain can also flush blooms out. Forecasting, once reliant on water sampling and hydrodynamic models, increasingly combines observation from satellites and aircraft with machine learning.

nature-eco-663.title: The environmental costs of fertilizer
nature-eco-663.text: Only a fraction of nitrogen fertilizer becomes plant matter. The rest accumulates in soil or is lost as runoff, and runoff from farmland is a major contributor to freshwater eutrophication. Greenhouse gases from manufacture and use of nitrogen fertilizer are about 5% of anthropogenic emissions, one third from production and two thirds from use. Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, which supplies energy and methane for the hydrogen used in Haber process ammonia. Phosphate fertilizers can add toxic elements to soil: cadmium in monoammonium phosphate ranged from 0.14 to 50.9 mg/kg, and fluoride from fluorapatite has risen in soils. Excess fertilizer may break down symbiosis between plant roots and mycorrhizal fungi, while effects on soil animals are still debated. Overapplication can cause fertilizer burn, damaging or killing the plant.

nature-eco-667.title: The Green Revolution: gains and trade-offs
nature-eco-667.text: Few agricultural changes are praised and blamed so loudly. Its effects on hunger, income, health and the environment are mixed and argued over. A 2012 review found it contributed to widespread poverty reduction, averted hunger for millions and avoided converting thousands of hectares to cultivation. A 2021 study found it substantially raised income: a ten-year delay would have cost 17% of GDP per capita, and no Green Revolution could have halved developing-world GDP per capita. A 2020 study of 37 developing countries found modern crop varieties reduced infant mortality by 2.4-5.3 percentage points from a baseline of 18%. Critics answer that more food is not the same as reliable access to enough food. The shift brought malnutrition such as iron and vitamin-A deficiencies, with crops grown in single-crop fields often exported, fed to animals or made into fuel. Malthusian critics call it unsustainable, yet a 2021 study found it reduced population growth rather than increasing it. Effects on wild biodiversity are disputed. Higher yields may spare land, but worn-out land and nutrient depletion pushed farmers to clear forest to keep production up. Studies indicate it substantially raised CO2 emissions, while a 2021 study found it cut the land used for agriculture. Its yield gains have been declining as social and environmental costs become clearer; the Evergreen Revolution aims at 'productivity in perpetuity without associated ecological harm'. Scholars disagree about the net effects on biodiversity, access to food and the environment.

nature-eco-669.title: Cutting methane emissions
nature-eco-669.text: Capturing and using methane can deliver environmental and economic benefits together. The IEA says about 40% of fossil-fuel methane emissions, 9% of all human methane emissions, could be eliminated at no net cost to firms with existing technology. The US EPA's 1996 Landfill Rule requires large landfills to collect and burn the gas landfills give off, though it excludes 96% of US landfills. Satellites such as Sentinel-5P, at about 50 square kilometre resolution, monitor emissions; MethaneSAT aims for 1 kilometre.

nature-eco-672.title: Non-trophic interactions: relationships beyond eating
nature-eco-672.text: Not every link between species is a meal. Non-trophic interactions are those that are not feeding relationships, such as habitat modification, mutualism and competition for space. They can indirectly change food web topology and the flow of energy through feeding links by affecting the species in the network and the strength of trophic links. Researchers argue that trophic and non-trophic interactions should be integrated in ecological network analysis. The few empirical studies cover a limited number of coastal systems, so it is unclear how far the findings generalize.

nature-eco-675.title: Nitrous oxide: the third greenhouse gas
nature-eco-675.text: Per molecule over 100 years, nitrous oxide traps 265 times as much heat as CO2. Its concentration is under one thousandth of CO2's, so its warming contribution is less than one third that of carbon dioxide. It is a minor atmospheric gas that is an active part of the planetary {{ref:nature-eco-176}} and a long-lived {{ref:nature-eco-162}}. It is the third most important such gas for global warming and has been a major ozone-depleting substance. Atmospheric abundance has grown more than 20% from about 270 ppb in 1750, surpassing 330 ppb in 2017, and is rising about 1 ppb per year. About 40% of emissions are human-caused, with growth chiefly from expanding agriculture. Annual human emissions equal about 3 billion tonnes of CO2 in warming effect. Microbes produce it by {{ref:nature-eco-395}}, {{ref:nature-eco-396}} and nitrifier denitrification.

nature-eco-678.title: Permafrost: frozen ground that is starting to thaw
nature-eco-678.text: Under the Arctic lies a freezer holding more carbon than anyone wants released. Permafrost is soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays below 0 degrees C continuously for two years or more. It lies beneath an active layer that freezes and thaws each year and supports plant growth. Its depth ranges from under a metre to 1,493 m in the Lena and Yana basins of Siberia. It is discontinuous where mean annual soil surface temperature is between -5 and 0 degrees C, and subsea permafrost lies on polar continental shelves. Only shallow-rooted plants survive on it, and black spruce dominates where it is extensive. Ice-rich thaw creates thermokarst landforms such as thermokarst lakes, thaw slumps and gullies. The ground is warming: permafrost warmed about 0.3 degrees C globally between 2007 and 2016. That deepens the active layer and releases stored carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, a positive climate feedback sometimes counted as a tipping point. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates permafrost emissions could equal 14-175 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide per degree of warming, against about 40 billion tonnes of annual human emissions by 2019. People are exposed too. As of 2021, 1162 Arctic settlements with about 5 million people sit on permafrost, and the ground under 42% of them is expected to thaw by 2050. Deep permafrost was once used to dispose of toxic waste, and about 4500 Arctic industrial facilities process or store hazardous chemicals there as of 2023.

nature-eco-683.title: Sediment transport: how flows move grains
nature-eco-683.text: Sediment transport is the movement of sediment by flowing water, wind or ice, set by the strength of the flow and the particle's size, volume, density and shape. Stronger flows raise lift and drag on a particle, while larger or denser particles tend to fall out of the flow. Water can move larger sediment than air because it is denser and more viscous. Typical rivers carry sand and gravel, and large floods carry cobbles and boulders. The Exner equation balances sediment in transport against deposition on the bed. Dams make a river pool and deposit its whole load, while taking out a dam or a fall in base level causes erosion.

nature-eco-685.title: Lavakas: the gullies that bleed Madagascar red
nature-eco-685.text: On Madagascar's high plateau, rivers run dark red-brown. The cause is the stripping of vegetation, which has opened gullies called lavakas. Slash-and-burn farming and rotating-plot farming of tropical forests are one cause of high loads of {{ref:nature-eco-682}}, because bare, seared ground is open to wind and water erosion. Some areas have as many as 150 lavakas per square kilometre, and lavakas may account for 84% of all sediments carried off by rivers. Siltation also brings fish kills, along with the costs of managing sediment and siltation.

nature-eco-694.title: Bacteria that signal contamination
nature-eco-694.text: Some bacteria are harmless themselves, but their presence in waste warns of other pathogens. Common indicators are total coliforms, fecal coliforms, E. coli and enterococci, and coliforms in surface water indicate fecal contamination. Microorganisms are abundant and easy to sample. Some make stress proteins when exposed to contaminants such as cadmium and benzene, an early warning. Helminth eggs indicate the safety of using wastewater again because they are the most resistant pathogens and survive 10-12 months in tropical climates.

nature-eco-699.title: Controlled burns: fighting fire with fire
nature-eco-699.text: Managers sometimes light fires on purpose. A controlled or prescribed burn is a fire set deliberately to remove built-up vegetation and decaying organic material from a landscape. Uses include tending forests, restoring ecosystems to health, land clearing and wildfire fuel management. Burns are usually done in cooler months. Fire can stimulate germination of some trees, and in grassland it shifts species towards natives and removes invasives. Planning stresses safety, preventing escape and limiting smoke. Back burning against the wind gives a slower, controllable fire and a black line. Indigenous peoples use fire worldwide, and it has been used to clear land since the Neolithic. The risk is real: the Calf Canyon/Hermits Peak Fire, New Mexico's largest wildfire, began from two US Forest Service controlled burns that got out of control and merged.

nature-eco-713.title: The Forest Stewardship Council: certifying wood
nature-eco-713.text: Look for the FSC mark on paper or timber and you are seeing a market-based answer to {{ref:nature-eco-053}}. The Forest Stewardship Council is an international non-profit, multistakeholder organization founded in 1993 that promotes responsible care of forests through timber certification. It runs a global certification system for forests and forest products. Members join one of three chambers: environmental, social and economic. Governments cannot be members and engage only as land owners. FSC does not audit itself. It accredits certification bodies, which then certify forests and companies to its standards. In September 2012 some 165 million hectares in 80 countries were certified, and about 24,000 chain of custody certificates were active in 107 countries. The main competing system is PEFC, criticized for little local or environmental organization influence and lack of transparency.

nature-eco-720.title: Remote sensing in hydrology: watching water from above
nature-eco-720.text: Remote sensing gives information on hydrologic processes where in situ sensors are sparse, and over large spatial extents. It can measure surface water storage, soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and snow and ice. Sources include land-based, airborne and satellite sensors using microwave, thermal and near-infrared data or laser scanning that times reflected light pulses.

nature-eco-729.title: Methanogenesis: how microbes make methane
nature-eco-729.text: Where oxygen is absent, one group of microbes finishes the job of decay and exhales methane. Methanogenesis is the formation of methane coupled to the capture of energy by microbes called methanogens. It is the final stage of anaerobic digestion and the final step in decomposing biomass in anoxic environments. Methanogens come only from the domain Archaea. They respire anaerobically, oxygen inhibits them, and carbon is the terminal electron acceptor. The two best-known pathways use acetic acid or carbon dioxide. Without methanogenesis, a great deal of carbon as fermentation products would accumulate in anaerobic environments. Flooded soils such as rice fields and wetlands are natural methane sources, though aerating them raises sulfates and nitrates that reduce methane production. Methanogenesis is also the main pathway breaking down landfilled organic matter, and the methane can be collected as fuel gas.

nature-eco-734.title: Methanotrophs: microbes that eat methane
nature-eco-734.text: Some microbes live on the gas that warms the planet. Methanotrophs are prokaryotes that metabolize {{ref:nature-eco-727}} as their source of carbon and chemical energy. They are bacteria or archaea that can grow aerobically or anaerobically, and are common where methane is produced, such as wetlands, soils, rice paddies, landfills and aquatic systems. They matter for global warming because they reduce the amount of methane emitted to the atmosphere in the global methane budget. Aerobic methanotrophs include Type I and X (Gammaproteobacteria, RuMP pathway) and Type II (Alphaproteobacteria, serine pathway). No aerobic methanotrophic archaea are known. Methane consumption without oxygen in marine sediments is mainly done by consortia of methane-oxidizing archaea and sulfate-reducing bacteria. They also have uses. In wastewater plants, methanotroph mixes could cut costs, raise nitrogen removal and produce useful biomolecules, and Methylococcus capsulatus makes animal feed from natural gas.

nature-eco-735.title: Ocean deoxygenation: the sea is losing its breath
nature-eco-735.text: The oceans have lost 1-2% of their oxygen since the mid-20th century. Ocean deoxygenation is the human-caused reduction of oxygen in parts of the ocean. It occurs in two settings: coastal zones, where eutrophication drives oxygen to very low levels, creating dead zones, and the open and deep ocean, where low-oxygen layers of the water are expanding. On the coast, nutrients from urban and agricultural runoff, worsened by deforestation, fuel productivity. The sinking organic matter is respired, using up oxygen and causing hypoxia or anoxia. Warmer water holds less oxygen, so ocean warming adds to the loss and compounds coastal eutrophication. Open ocean areas with no oxygen have grown by more than 1.7 million square miles in 50 years, and coastal low-oxygen areas have grown tenfold. Since 1950 more than 500 coastal sites have reported oxygen below 2 mg per litre, the usual hypoxia threshold. Models predict up to 7% decline in global ocean oxygen over the next hundred years. Less oxygen affects productivity, nutrient and carbon cycling and habitat function, threatening marine life and the people who depend on it for food or livelihood.

nature-eco-739.title: Seascape ecology: reading patterns in the sea
nature-eco-739.text: A seagrass bed in a sand flat is not just a place; it is a pattern. Seascape ecology studies the causes and ecological consequences of spatial pattern in the marine environment, borrowing the frameworks used to study patterns on land. Its central tenet is that patch context matters: surroundings shape local conditions, so the shape, size, arrangement and edges of patches all count. Studies choose scales that fit an organism's movement. Juvenile fish use several habitats as they grow, so ignoring mangrove roots, macroalgae or seagrass can mislead assessments of an estuary. The field has grown since the 1970s, yet in marine systems understanding is still in its infancy.

nature-eco-742.title: The water table: where the ground turns wet
nature-eco-742.text: Dig deep enough almost anywhere and the ground turns wet. The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation, below which ground pores are filled with groundwater. Above it lies the vadose zone. Below it, permeable rock layers that yield groundwater are described in {{ref:nature-res-112}}. It is not the same as the water level in a confined deeper layer of such rock, which is the potentiometric surface. The table rises and falls seasonally with precipitation and evapotranspiration, and where it reaches the surface, springs, rivers, lakes and oases occur. Groundwater entering rivers and lakes supplies their base-flow water levels. People change it. Fossil water, held for millennia mainly in deserts, is not renewed by rainfall, so extraction permanently changes the table. Crops need a minimum depth: cotton in the Nile Delta is sensitive and needs a deep table, while wheat tolerates 45 cm. Near the coast, lower tables from heavier water use have let seawater contaminate groundwater, as in Libya and Israel.

nature-eco-743.title: Woody plant encroachment: when shrubs take over grassland
nature-eco-743.text: Open grassland can quietly turn into scrub. Woody plant encroachment is the spread and thickening of native shrubs and bushes at the expense of grasses and forbs. It concerns native plants, not alien invasives, and can shift open grasslands and savannas to closed woodlands. It affects an estimated 500 million hectares on all continents, and the UNCCD names it a key contributor to rangeland loss. Causes include overgrazing, suppressed wildfires, fewer wild herbivores, land abandonment, and possibly climate change. Once established, shrubs suppress grass. The result is a form of land degradation harming biodiversity, the refilling of groundwater, carbon storage and herbivore carrying capacity. The cost is economic too: in the western United States, rangeland tree expansion has cost producers an estimated $5 billion since 1990. Encroached grasslands can be a stable state that does not return on its own, and restoring them is difficult.

nature-eco-747.title: Kinds of natural selection
nature-eco-747.text: Selection can be sorted in several ways: by its effect on a trait, on the variety of genes in a population, by life cycle stage, by unit of selection, or by resource competed for. Stabilizing selection holds a trait at an optimum, while directional selection favours extreme values. Purifying selection removes genetic variation; balancing selection maintains it through negative frequency-dependent selection. Viability selection raises survival probability, and fecundity selection raises reproductive rate. Sexual selection is competition for mates. It typically proceeds via fecundity selection, sometimes at the expense of viability.

nature-eco-750.title: Cities and gene flow: fragmentation or connection
nature-eco-750.text: Cities can split populations or join them. Two models describe how city growth affects {{ref:nature-eco-748}}: the splitting of habitat into isolated patches, which lowers genetic variety, and urban facilitation, which connects populations. Facilitation reduces isolation and brings previously separated species into contact, directly or indirectly. Whether corridors work depends on species' dispersal abilities and their adaptiveness to anthropogenic structures.

nature-eco-753.title: The intermediate disturbance hypothesis
nature-eco-753.text: Diversity peaks, the hypothesis says, when things are shaken up a moderate amount. The intermediate disturbance hypothesis holds that the local variety of species is highest when ecological disturbance is neither too rare nor too frequent. At low disturbance, competitive species push others to extinction. At high disturbance, all species risk extinction. At intermediate levels, species of early and late successional stages coexist, because moderate disturbance prevents interspecific competition from running to exclusion. K-selected species dominate stable ecosystems, and r-selected species colonize recently cleared areas. Occasional disturbance lets both live together. It is a nonequilibrium model, with Connell usually cited as its founder, and its hump-backed graph shows diversity against disturbance. The idea is contested. The terms intermediate and disturbance are ambiguous: what counts depends on the system's disturbance history and on whether frequency, extent, intensity or duration is evaluated. The marine Menge-Sutherland model also showed a discrepancy with it.

nature-eco-757.title: The paradox of enrichment
nature-eco-757.text: Feeding the prey can doom the predator. The paradox of enrichment is the idea that increasing the food available to a prey species can destabilize the predator's population. Michael Rosenzweig coined it in 1971. Enrichment was modelled as a higher {{ref:nature-eco-593}} for the prey, which can make the equilibrium unstable, usually giving a limit cycle. The predator boom can crash and may lead to local eradication or extinction of the predator. Past a critical level of it the system undergoes a Hopf bifurcation. The result is counterintuitive, hence 'paradox'. Support comes mainly from small laboratory experiments, with limited field support. Destabilisation need not occur with inedible, invulnerable or unpalatable prey, a ratio-dependent functional response such as the Arditi-Ginzburg model, spatial heterogeneity, inducible defense, or density-dependent predator mortality.

nature-eco-758.title: Population pyramids: reading a population's age shape
nature-eco-758.text: A population pyramid is a graph of a population's distribution by age group and sex, usually for a country or region. Males are conventionally on the left and females on the right, with bars in absolute numbers or percentages. In ecology it shows a population's age distribution, hinting at reproductive capability and likelihood of continuation. A broad base signals fertility above replacement, and the shape also reveals the age-dependency ratio of those too young or old to work. Pyramids fall into three types: stationary, with births and deaths roughly balanced; expansive, wide at young ages; and constrictive, narrowed at the bottom. Their shape tracks the {{ref:nature-eecon-250}}: more developed countries sit in stages three to five, least developed in stages one and two.

nature-eco-760.title: Population viability analysis: forecasting extinction risk
nature-eco-760.text: How likely is a population to vanish within a set number of years? Population viability analysis is a species-specific risk assessment method in conservation biology that gives that probability. It combines species characteristics and environmental variability to forecast population health and extinction risk, and each analysis is built for one target population. Managers use it to judge urgency of recovery, find key life stages, compare management options and assess impacts of habitat loss. Mark Shaffer's 1978 grizzly bear model at Yellowstone calculated extinction probabilities and a minimum viable population size. US use grew with {{ref:nature-pol-159}}. One analysis of Fender's blue butterfly found it more at risk than thought and located key recovery sites. Another, of the Santa Catalina island fox, found it highly susceptible to catastrophes more often than once every 20 years. Critics note that a precise forecast T years ahead may need five to ten times T years of data, and suitable data exist for only 2% of threatened birds. Retrospective tests show projections are accurate with sound or long-term data. Its value lies more in assessing threats than in making long-term categorical predictions, and debates over its proper uses remain unresolved.

nature-econ-141.title: Preferences: how people rank their options
nature-econ-141.text: Taste and need, not price, availability or income, decide what a person wants most. In economics, a preference is the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, from most to least wanted. Most models of decision-making share one basic principle, transitivity: anyone who prefers A to B and B to C should prefer A to C. An ordering that is both transitive and complete is called rational, and people who follow one are called rational agents. Real people do not always behave this way. Their preferences can form cycles with no best choice. Most economic models assume preferences stay stable, an assumption long disputed outside the school described in {{ref:nature-hist-023}}. In fact preferences shift with new technology and social influence, as when friends at lunch shift each other's food choices. Ragnar Frisch first expressed preferences in mathematical form for demand and utility theory in 1926.

nature-econ-151.title: Absolute advantage: simply being better at it
nature-econ-151.text: Suppose the UK needs fewer hours to make cloth and Portugal fewer to make wine. By specializing and trading, both end up with more of each good. That is absolute advantage at work: the ability of a person, firm or country to produce a good or service more efficiently than others. Adam Smith first described it in The Wealth of Nations in 1776. Arguing against {{ref:nature-hist-022}}, he said all nations could gain from trading freely and specializing. Yet a party can lack an absolute advantage in anything and still gain from trade, through the principle covered in {{ref:nature-econ-106}}.

nature-econ-153.title: Economic systems: who owns, who decides
nature-econ-153.text: Scarcity forces every society to answer the same questions: what to produce, how to produce it and who gets what is produced. An economic system is the way a society organizes the production, allocation and distribution of goods and services to answer them. Systems are usually classed along two lines: who owns the means of production, and whether resources are allocated through markets or planning. Private ownership with markets is market capitalism. Public or cooperative ownership with planning is a socialist {{ref:nature-econ-849}}. Public ownership with markets is market socialism. Sorted by how they allocate resources, systems include market, mixed, planned, traditional, subsistence and gift economies. Capitalism combines private ownership of the means of production with markets to coordinate the economy. History has tested the alternatives. By the 1990s most communist states had ended or reformed their central planning, moving toward markets.

nature-econ-155.title: Criticisms of neoclassical economics: the case against the mainstream
nature-econ-155.text: Thorstein Veblen mocked the neoclassical view of a person as "a lightning calculator of pleasures and pains." He was far from alone. Marxist, behavioral, Austrian, post-Keynesian, institutionalist and other schools each break with neoclassical economics, and insiders such as Joseph Stiglitz criticize it too. The main target is its assumption of rational, self-interested, fully informed people. Behavioral economists study how real decisions differ from that picture. Hayek argued that by assuming full information, its equilibrium models assume away the real problem: discovering knowledge spread among many people. Critics also say it carries a normative bias while claiming to be value-free, and they call for more pluralistic teaching. Because it holds that market exchange usually allocates goods best, critics charge that it promotes commodification, turning things into goods for sale, and the shift of public services into private hands. Defenders reply that it is also the main tool for judging how policies affect inequality. Schools still disagree over whether its assumptions and mathematical methods are sound, and whether modern mainstream models have moved beyond it.

nature-econ-200.title: Productive efficiency: no waste on the production line
nature-econ-200.text: An economy can make things cheaply and still make the wrong things. Productive efficiency is a situation in which an economy, using today's technology, cannot make more of one good without making less of another. Every point on the production possibility frontier meets the test. An economy falls inside its frontier when capital or labor sit idle or are put into the wrong industries. In long-run perfect competition, each good is made at the lowest point of its average total cost curve, where marginal cost equals average total cost. Productive efficiency says nothing about making the right mix of goods; misapplied, it can produce the wrong basket faster and cheaper. Monopolies may fall short through {{ref:nature-econ-853}}, though economies of scale can sometimes let them charge less than competitive firms. Better technology and management can push the frontier outward. Data envelopment analysis and stochastic frontier analysis are the most popular ways to estimate it.

nature-econ-308.title: Isoquants: many routes to the same output
nature-econ-308.text: A factory can make the same output with many workers and few machines, or few workers and many machines. An isoquant is the curve joining all the combinations of inputs that produce the same quantity of output. Drawn with two inputs such as labor and capital on its axes, it is a level set of the production function, a slice taken at one output. It is the producer's counterpart of an indifference curve, except that output can be measured exactly in physical units. Its slope is {{ref:nature-eecon-257}}, the rate at which one input can replace the other. Because that rate diminishes, isoquants bow toward the origin. Perfect-substitute inputs give straight isoquants; perfect complements give L-shaped ones with a kink at the fixed ratio. The cheapest input mix lies where an isoquant touches an isocost line, a line of equal spending. There the ratio of marginal products equals the ratio of input prices. Two isoquants never cross.

nature-econ-339.title: Consumer surplus: the bargain buyers get
nature-econ-339.text: Water for drinking usually carries a large consumer surplus, because people would pay very high prices for it to survive. Consumer surplus is the gap between the most a buyer would be willing to pay for something and the price they actually pay. The first few liters of water are worth the most, since they prevent death, so they hold more surplus than later liters. That points to the general source of the surplus. Buyers value each extra unit less than the last, yet pay the same market price for every unit. On a graph, consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve and above the price; with a straight-line demand curve it is a triangle. A rise in consumer surplus after a price change is read as a gain in welfare, a fall as a loss. When supply grows and the price falls, existing buyers gain on the units they already bought, and new buyers enter and gain too.

nature-econ-364.title: Oligopoly: a market run by a few
nature-econ-364.text: Civil aviation, electricity supply, telecommunications, sugar refining, beer making, and pulp and paper have all been cited as oligopolies: markets in which a few sellers control pricing. A duopoly is the smallest case, an oligopoly of only two firms. In such markets each firm's actions affect the others and provoke reactions, so the firms are mutually interdependent. That makes cooperation tempting. Oligopolists often turn to {{ref:nature-econ-857}} to maximize profits, by price-fixing or by forming price-fixing groups ({{ref:nature-econ-301}}) that keep new firms out. Competition laws mostly catch formal agreements to do so, so firms can escape by coordinating tacitly, without any explicit deal.
